newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden cannot accept EU alcohol proposal - Monti.
newsitem.headline: Sweden cannot accept EU alcohol proposal - Monti.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it could extend the final deadline for ending Nordic restrictions on personal alcohol imports until the end of July 2002, but that Sweden had declared it could not accept this.

European Union Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti, speaking after a meeting with ministers from Denmark, Sweden and Finland, said Finland and Denmark could accept the proposed deadline even though they would prefer the year 2004.
"It (the year 2002) is the furthest we can in hoping to reach a consensus among member states," Monti told reporters.
He said there would be flexibility in how the Nordics phased out their restrictions, leaving it up to them to decide about the details.

He met Swedish Taxation Minister Thomas Ostros, Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto and Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved in Strasbourg, France, on the sidelines of the regular meeting of the European Parliament.

Monti said he hoped to see them again shortly but that Sweden was opposing setting any final date for ending the restrictions on the amount of alcohol Swedes may bring in from other countries in the bloc.
Monti has always insisted on the necessity of an agreed deadline.
The Commission will be drafting a proposal on the issue to the November meeting of EU finance ministers in Brussels.
Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict imports of cheaper alcohol, but these will expire by the end of 1996, the Commission says.

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they break the rules of the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while the Nordics want to extend them for health and tax reasons.

The issue is politically sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking. It is also a question of fiscal importance as the taxes bring in much needed revenue.
Alcohol and tobacco taxes bring in about $2.7 billion annually for Sweden and $2.17 billion for Finland.

A compromise leading to a phasing out of the restrictions would gradually allow Swedes, Finns and Danes to take home more alcohol while at the same giving the three states time to prepare for the new rules, the Commission says.
But as Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict them.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer, much less than most other EU citizens.
